title: LLM Inference Latency: Why Round-Trip Time Is the Wrong Metric, and What to Measure Instead
summary: Round-trip time hides poor LLM inference latency. Learn why TTFT, inter-token latency, and tail latency matter, and how edge GPUs fix it.
body_markdown:
Round-trip time looks like the obvious number to watch for LLM inference latency. It isn't. A connection can post a perfectly good RTT while the actual experience, the time before a user sees the first word, the gap between each word after that, and the worst-case delay on the slowest requests, is bad. According to DriveNets, which provides the network fabric for WhiteFiber ContinuumTM, fixing LLM inference latency starts with measuring the right things and deploying GPUs in the right place.


‍


## What Actually Drives **LLM Inference Latency**


‍


Three metrics that matter more than round-trip delay for inference workloads:


‍


1. ` Time to first token (TTFT)` – how long a user waits before anything appears
2. ` Inter-token latency` – the gap between each token as a response streams
3. ` Tail latency` – how bad the worst-case requests get, not just the average


‍


Optimizing only for round-trip time can leave all three of these unaddressed. The fix isn't a faster backbone between a central cluster and the user. It's deploying GPU infrastructure closer to the customer, at the edge of the network, and distributing that infrastructure across multiple sites using scale-across networking so the workload runs across the entire network rather than from one distant location.


‍


‍


## How WhiteFiber **Puts This Into Production**


‍


WhiteFiber Continuum links QTS ATL1 (Atlanta) and QTS SUW1 (Suwanee) facilities, 83 kilometers apart, over 12 dark fiber strands leased from Zayo, delivering **136 Tbps of aggregate bandwidth at 0.9 milliseconds of round-trip latency** across that span. That low, consistent latency is what makes distributing inference across sites viable in the first place, since the cross-site link has to behave like part of one network, not a slow hop to a remote location.


‍


The network interconnect is powered by DriveNets AI Fabric, built on Broadcom's Jericho3-AI and Ramon3 chipsets, using scheduled cell-based Ethernet instead of hash-based load balancing. Cells spray evenly across every link, with HBM-buffered leaf switches at the site boundary absorbing traffic bursts before they turn into the kind of jitter that shows up as inconsistent inter-token latency.


‍


On the storage side, WEKA NeuralMesh pulls exactly the data a given job needs to the site where its GPU allocation lands, so inference workloads aren't waiting on data that lives somewhere else.


‍


Complete inference cells can run close to users and data, keeping the token-serving path local, while scale-across still handles request routing, spillover, model distribution, and recovery across sites behind the scenes.


‍


‍

‍


‍


DriveNets, which operates the AI fabric layer for WhiteFiber Continuum, explains what it actually takes to reduce LLM inference latency and which metrics tell the real story.Watch here


‍


> In DriveNets' words: "In order to reduce the latency associated with inference workload, . . . deploy these GPUs closer to the customer at the edge of the network. In order to do that, . . . distribute your GPU infrastructure across multiple sites and use scale-across in order to distribute the workload across the entire network. . . . Measure time to first token, tail latency, time between tokens, not just round-trip delay in order to make everything work."


‍


‍


## Beyond Two Sites: **Scaling Inference Further**


‍


Continuum runs on two sites today, with the Jericho3-AI chipset underneath supporting a single cluster of up to 32,000 GPUs at 800Gbps each, 62 times the 512 GPUs running across ATL1 and SUW1 today. For LLM inference latency specifically, more sites mean more places to serve users from, extending the same scale-across model into a hub-and-spoke or mesh configuration rather than requiring a new, separately managed deployment at every new edge location.


‍


‍


## Who Needs to **Solve It**


‍


LLM inference latency matters most to:


‍


1. ` Large-scale consumer products` such as streaming, gaming, or AI-powered media that need to be close to more than one population of end users at once
2. ` Telco and edge operators` monetizing existing distributed infrastructure, central offices and fiber investment, as low-latency inference capacity
3. ` Frontier model labs and AI research teams` serving inference from more than one site rather than a single, distant cluster
4. ` GPUaaS and NeoCloud providers` that need to back inference SLAs with real architecture, not just proximity claims


‍


‍


‍


‍


## **FAQ**


‍


#### **What is LLM inference latency?**


‍


> LLM inference latency is the delay a user experiences when interacting with a large language model, measured by time to first token, inter-token latency, and tail latency, rather than round-trip network delay alone.


‍


#### **Why is round-trip time the wrong metric here?**


‍


> Round-trip time can look fine while the metrics users actually notice, how long before the first word appears, how evenly tokens stream after that, and how bad the worst-case requests get, are still poor. Optimizing only for RTT can leave all three unaddressed.


‍


#### **How do you reduce it?**


‍


> Reducing LLM inference latency means deploying GPUs closer to the customer at the edge of the network, distributing that GPU infrastructure across multiple sites with scale-across networking, and measuring time to first token, inter-token latency, and tail latency instead of relying on round-trip delay alone.


‍


#### **How does WhiteFiber Continuum help reduce LLM inference latency?**


‍


> Continuum connects two QTS facilities 83 kilometers apart using DriveNets AI Fabric for the network layer and WEKA NeuralMesh for data and storage, delivering 136 Tbps of aggregate bandwidth at 0.9 milliseconds of round-trip latency, letting complete inference cells run close to users while scale-across handles routing, spillover, and recovery across sites.


‍


#### **Is this approach to LLM inference latency available today?**


‍


> Yes. WhiteFiber Continuum has been commercially available since September 23, 2026, built in collaboration with DriveNets and WEKA.


‍


#### **Can this approach scale beyond two sites?**


‍


> Yes. The Jericho3-AI chipset underneath Continuum has headroom for a single cluster of up to 32,000 GPUs, and additional sites are expected to join in a hub-and-spoke or mesh configuration, extending low-latency inference coverage to more locations using the same networking approach already in place.
